_comment: Shared cases for the two figures each client formats for itself (#619, ADR-0011's
fourth family): a token count and a relative age. They stay client-side because
they are presentation, and an age is a function of *now* — a value the daemon
would freeze at the moment it was sent.
Duplicated is not unchecked. internal/tui/format_shared_test.go and
test/js/dashboard.test.mjs both read this file and must agree case for case.
The tokens section is why this fixture exists. Before it, Go printed 1250 as
'1.2k' and JavaScript as '1.3k' — %.1f rounds half to even, toFixed rounds half
away from zero — and Go kept the '.0' JavaScript trimmed. Both sides had a green
test, because each had picked cases where its own implementation was right and
the case that separated them was in neither list.
Two rules settled here: one decimal is always kept, because the terminal column
is aligned on a character grid and a width that changes with the value breaks it;
and the half rounds away from zero, which is what a reader expects.
The cases ending in 50 are there because the first attempt at this fix passed
the eleven cases above it and still disagreed on 4004 values in the first three
million: dividing into a float and rounding the result rounds twice, and the two
languages land on different sides. Both now compute an integer count of tenths.
One boundary is deliberately NOT claimed here: a timestamp that is not RFC3339
at all. Go's parser is strict and answers '-', while Date.parse accepts a bare
'2026-08-27' and dates it. Nothing emits such a value today, and #629 is where
the daemon starts refusing one; asserting an agreement that does not exist would
be worse than naming the gap.

tokens.why: below the first threshold the count is shown whole
still whole one below the threshold
the decimal is kept on a round value — the column must not change width
the half rounds away from zero, not to even
a count ending in 50 is the case a float divide gets wrong: 1150/1000 is 1.14999… and rounding it twice lifts it to 1.2 in one language and not the other
the same trap one step up
and where it crosses a whole unit
a round thousand keeps its decimal too
one below a million is still counted in thousands
the million threshold switches unit and keeps the decimal
millions round by the same rule
the ending-in-50 trap exists in millions too
and no rounding needed in millions either

age.why: no timestamp at all is a dash, never a zero
an unreadable timestamp is a dash too
the truncation is toward zero, not to the nearest
one second short of an hour is still minutes
one second short of a day is still hours
a timestamp in the future is clamped to zero, not shown negative
an offset is honoured, not read as UTC
